edits.note: U1 of an 11-unit plan and a likely first exposure either way. 'This is the text-encounter unit for the chapter, so unhurried reading aloud is the priority' says why without naming what follows

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Informational Narrative

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the chapter setting — Firozabad, Uttar Pradesh, India's glassware hub — by asking children what they know about bangles and how they might be made. This brief discussion activates prior knowledge and builds curiosity.

The teacher reads the entire informational narrative aloud at a steady, expressive pace, pausing briefly at the introduction of Ravi, the arrival of Ananya, and the Diwali collection episode. Children follow along in their textbooks (pp.119–133).

The teacher invites three or four children to take turns reading a paragraph aloud, supporting fluency and pronunciation of key words such as artisan, furnace, geometric, intergenerational, and transportation.

The teacher closes by asking one open question: 'What surprised you most in this story?' and takes two or three brief spoken responses to confirm that children have grasped the broad shape of the narrative.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the text-encounter unit for the chapter, so unhurried reading aloud is the priority. Watch for mispronunciation of 'Firozabad' and 'geometric'; model these once before the shared-reading portion. The chapter's informational register may feel denser than a narrative; pace the read-aloud deliberately to let children build a mental picture of the workshop.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: Ravi, Ananya, and the Community

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.123): answer three questions on bangle-making, Ananya's role, and community impact.

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites a quick choral re-reading of the paragraph describing glass being heated and shaped in Ravi's furnace (pp.119–120), refreshing the production process in children's minds before comprehension work begins.

Let us Think — A. (p.123): the teacher poses question 1 ('How were glass bangles made in Ravi's small workshop?') and facilitates a whole-class discussion, charting key steps — heating glass, shaping into bangles, adding colour and designs — on the board.

Let us Think — A. (p.123): question 2 ('Who was Ananya? How did she help Ravi?') is discussed in pairs before two or three pairs share aloud; the teacher draws out the idea of modern floral and geometric patterns complementing traditional designs.

Let us Think — A. (p.123): question 3 ('How did the success of the new bangles help the community?') is taken up whole-class; children articulate the ripple effect — more work for artisans, jobs in packing and transportation — before writing one-sentence answers in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the narrative of Ravi's workshop and Ananya's contribution, children are now working through the textbook's three comprehension questions in sequence. A common gap at this stage is conflating Ananya's role with Ravi's — prompt children explicitly to distinguish her contribution (modern design) from his (traditional craft and workshop management). Accept spoken answers before written ones; the oral discussion scaffolds the written sentence.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss: Design, Pride, and Festival Markets

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.123): guided discussion on design ideas, a proud creative experience, and festival market lists.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.123): the teacher poses question 1 — 'If you were in Ananya's place, what modern designs or colours would you add?' — and invites each child to whisper an idea to a partner first before sharing with the class; the teacher collects responses on the board as a class word-cloud of colours and patterns.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.123): question 2 — 'Have you ever created something that made you happy?' — is taken up through a structured go-round; each child names their creation (drawing, model, project, dish) in one sentence, and the teacher validates every contribution as a form of craft or making.

Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.123): question 3 — 'Make a list of things you buy from local markets during festivals' — is done first as a one-minute silent think-and-jot, then shared aloud in groups of three before the class pools a master list on the board.

The teacher draws the three strands together by pointing out how Ravi and Ananya's success benefited their community — connecting children's own festival-market lists to the real economic ripple described in the chapter — and invites one closing spoken sentence from three volunteers.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed how the bangle workshop creates community jobs, children are now connecting those themes to their own experiences of making and celebrating. Encourage children who are shy about 'creating something' to count any domestic contribution — helping decorate, packing sweets, drawing a card — as a valid creative act. The festival-market list works best as a genuine pooling of diverse regional experience; do not limit it to the examples the chapter mentions.

periods.activity_title: Listening: Besan Laddu Steps in Sequence

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.127): listen to the besan laddu passage and arrange five steps in correct sequence.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly introduces the besan laddu passage — telling children they will hear a short description of a family making a sweet and must track the order of steps carefully. Children are told to listen for words that signal sequence: 'first', 'then', 'when', 'finally'.

Let us Listen (p.127): the teacher reads the transcript aloud three times at a natural spoken pace, pausing between readings for children to make brief mental notes. On the third reading children may pencil a number next to each of the five printed steps in their textbook.

Children compare their sequencing with a partner, discussing any steps they placed differently; the teacher then invites one pair to read their sequence aloud and opens it for class verification, step by step.

Children write the five steps in the correct sequence in their notebooks in full sentences, and the teacher confirms the verified order: step 5 → 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 (i.e., family helps prepare → mother roasts flour → father adds ghee and sugar → Meera and Arjun shape → kids decorate). Any child whose sequence differs rechecks against the transcript on p.127.

periods.teacher_notes: The laddu passage is a sequencing task, not a comprehension-of-meaning task — children who understand every word may still muddle the order, which is the productive challenge here. Read at a natural but deliberate pace; resist slowing artificially or signalling the order change with heavy vocal stress. The five steps in the textbook are deliberately scrambled as a scaffold; remind children to use the signal words ('first', 'then', 'finally') rather than trying to recall the passage from memory alone.

periods.activity_title: Speaking: Crafts, Traditions, and Festival Links

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak B. (p.126): share a regional craft or tradition linked to festivals with the class.

time_bands.activity: The teacher connects the chapter's theme — glass bangles as a festival craft specific to Firozabad — to the wider idea that every region of India has its own festival craft or tradition. Two or three examples are elicited from children to warm up: earthen diyas, kolam, sewing of festival clothes, making garlands.

Let us Speak B. (p.126): children are given a quiet two-minute think about a craft or tradition from their own region that is linked to a festival. Each child then takes a brief turn to speak — naming the craft, the festival, and one detail about how it is made or performed.

After all volunteers have spoken, the teacher facilitates a short class discussion: 'Which crafts did more than one person mention? Which were completely new to the class?' Children compare the diversity of traditions they have just heard, practising the language of comparison ('In my region… but here…').

The teacher consolidates by noting that just as glass bangle-making in Firozabad sustains a whole community, regional festival crafts everywhere create livelihoods — linking the oral activity back to the chapter's community-impact theme.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard each other's festival experiences in the guided-conversation unit, children are now moving to individual descriptive speech grounded in regional knowledge. Accept responses in English even if phrased simply; the communicative goal is specificity — name the craft, name the festival, give one real detail. If a child cannot recall a regional craft, guide them gently toward a domestic festival practice (rangoli, cooking a special dish) rather than leaving them without a contribution.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.124): list three associated words each for Bangle, Factory, Friend, School.
Let us Learn (p.124): rewrite five sentences using correct capital letters, full stops, commas, and question marks.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn — A. (p.124): the teacher shows the completed example (Festivals — Joy, Sweets, Family) and asks children what connects those three words to 'Festivals'. Children then work in pairs to generate three associated words each for 'Bangle', 'Factory', 'Friend', and 'School', jotting them in their notebooks.

Pairs share their associations with the class for 'Bangle' and 'Factory'; the teacher collates responses on the board and discusses how each word creates a web of meaning — linking 'Bangle' to the chapter's world of colour, festivals, and craft.

Let us Learn — B. (p.124): the teacher displays the five unpunctuated sentences on the board (or reads them aloud) and takes the first one together as a class, identifying where a capital letter and full stop are needed. Children then correct the remaining four sentences independently in their notebooks.

The teacher reads aloud the corrected version of each sentence and children mark their own work; brief discussion clarifies why sentence 3 and 5 take a question mark ('did Ravi…', 'did the customers…') while the others take a full stop.

periods.teacher_notes: Word associations are most productive when children reach slightly beyond the obvious — push 'Bangle' beyond just 'glass' and 'festival' toward sensory words (tinkle, colour, wrist) that the chapter itself uses. For the punctuation task, the most common error at this stage is forgetting the comma after an introductory phrase ('On Diwali night,'); draw attention to sentence 2 explicitly before children work independently.

periods.activity_title: Past Perfect Tense: First and Second Actions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.125): identify first and second action in five past-perfect sentences from context.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes on the board the anchor sentence from the textbook: 'Ananya had completed her schooling before she joined the factory.' Children identify the two actions aloud — completing schooling (earlier) and joining the factory (later) — and the teacher explains the structure: 'had + past participle' marks the action that finished first.

Let us Learn — C. (p.125): the teacher reads sentence 1 ('The crowd had dispersed when we reached the market') and asks children to circle the 'had + past participle' phrase (had dispersed) and underline the simple-past clause (reached). Children work in pairs on sentences 2 and 3, identifying first and second actions and writing them as 'First: ___ / Second: ___' in their notebooks.

Sentences 4 and 5 are taken up individually; children write first and second actions and the teacher circulates to check. A brief class comparison follows for any sentence where children disagreed on which action came first.
The teacher closes with one oral rapid-fire check: calls a sentence number and a child names either the first or second action, reinforcing the tense pattern in spoken form before the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with word associations and punctuation grounded in the chapter's language, children are now meeting the past perfect tense through the same textbook context — Ananya joining the factory is the chapter's own example and keeps the grammar anchored to a real scene. The most common confusion is reversing first and second action; insist that children write 'First: had + V' before writing 'Second: simple past' so the structural logic is visible in their notebooks. Sentence 3 ('When you rang the doorbell, I had switched off the TV') inverts the clause order — address this one together before asking children to attempt it independently.

periods.activity_title: Tongue Twisters: Speed and Accuracy Drill

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A. (p.124–125): practise five tongue twisters, increasing speed without errors.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the purpose of tongue twisters — training the mouth to move quickly between similar sounds — and models the first twister ('Red lorry blue lorry') slowly, then at medium pace, then quickly, inviting children to notice where their tongue trips.

Let us Speak — A. (pp.124–125): the class works through all five twisters chorally, starting very slowly for each one and building speed in three rounds. The teacher taps a rhythm on the desk to regulate pace; on the third round children go as fast as they can manage without stopping.

Children practise in pairs, taking turns to say each twister to their partner who listens for errors ('broke' said as 'broke' — fine; tongue stumble causing a sound swap — counts as a mistake). Pairs count how many perfect repetitions each child manages for their favourite twister.

Three or four volunteers perform a twister of their choice in front of the class at full speed; the class applauds and the teacher notes the specific sound pattern targeted by each twister ('b' in the Babli one, 'gr'/'gl' in the green-glass one).

periods.teacher_notes: Tongue twisters are phonological play, not a test — keep the atmosphere warm and competitive-in-fun rather than evaluative. 'Babli bought beautiful bangles but the bangles broke' links directly to the chapter's subject and can be used as a light callback to the craft world the class has been reading about. 'Green glass globes glow green' is the hardest for most Grade V children; allow extra slow-practice repetitions before the pair work on this one.

periods.activity_title: Festival Paragraph: Planning, Drafting, and Sharing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.128): plan and write an 80–100-word paragraph on a recently celebrated festival.

time_bands.activity: The teacher elicits the four hint categories on the board — special dish, meeting with friends and family, prayer, other ritual — and models a planning web for a sample festival, thinking aloud: 'My special dish was… We met… We prayed at…' Children copy the four headings and jot two or three words under each in their own notebooks.

The teacher reminds children of the target length (80–100 words) and models the first two sentences on the board as a shared-writing demonstration, showing how to turn notes into full sentences with connecting words ('first', 'then', 'after that').

Let us Write — A. (p.128): children draft their festival paragraphs independently in their notebooks. The teacher circulates, giving brief formative nudges — 'Can you add a sensory detail here?', 'Check your capital for the festival name' — without taking over the child's writing.
Three volunteers read their completed paragraphs aloud to the class. After each reading the teacher asks one peer to say one thing they noticed or liked — building a brief oral response habit.

Children do a self-count of their word total, mark it at the end of the paragraph, and check that they have addressed at least three of the four hint categories; any gap is filled with one extra sentence before the notebook is closed.

periods.teacher_notes: Having spoken about festival markets and regional traditions in earlier oracy work, children bring lived experience to this writing task — encourage them to write about a festival they personally celebrated rather than a generic account. At this stage, 80–100 words is an achievable target if children used the planning web; the most common shortfall is stopping after two or three sentences without developing any detail. A child who finishes quickly can be asked to add one more sensory detail — a smell, a sound, or the feel of a material.

periods.activity_title: Craft Geography, Regional Fame, and Rangoli Making

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.129): find and write which Indian place is famous for each of four crafts.
Let us Do — C. (p.130): follow step-by-step diagrams to create a star-pattern rangoli.

homework.task_brief: Let us Do — B. (p.129): find out what your State or Union Territory is famous for and prepare two sentences to share.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do — A. (p.129): the teacher briefly describes each of the four crafts — Madhubani painting (Bihar), Paithani Saree (Maharashtra), Blue pottery (Rajasthan / Jaipur), Phulkari embroidery (Punjab) — using the textbook photographs on p.129. Children write the craft-to-place matches in their notebooks; the teacher confirms answers and invites any child who has seen one of these crafts in real life to share a detail.

The teacher assigns the homework for this unit: find out what their own State or Union Territory is famous for and prepare two spoken sentences to share. Children note the task in their homework diaries.

Let us Do — C. (p.130): children open the textbook to the seven-step rangoli guide. The teacher walks through steps 1–3 on the board using dots to model the grid, then children begin working through all seven steps in their notebooks or on dot-grid paper. The teacher circulates to guide the dot-to-dot line connections that form the star pattern.

Children hold up their rangoli drawings; the teacher invites brief spoken observations — 'What pattern do you see forming?' — connecting the making activity to the chapter's celebration of craft and design.

periods.teacher_notes: The craft-geography task in Task A is a research-style match at this stage — children may not know the answers before looking, and that is the point; encourage them to treat the textbook photographs as their first clue. The rangoli activity requires fine motor patience; children who rush through the early dot-grid steps often lose the symmetry at step 5 or 6. Spending a little longer on steps 1–3 together before releasing children to work independently prevents most errors.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Craft, Community, and Creative Voices

time_bands.activity: Reading synthesis: the teacher puts three key moments on the board — (1) Ravi shaping bangles in the furnace, (2) Ananya introducing modern designs, (3) the Diwali collection's community ripple — and asks children to speak one sentence summarising each moment in their own words. This oral summary draws together the narrative arc of the whole informational text.

Oracy synthesis: in pairs, children retell the story of Ravi and Ananya's collaboration to each other — one child plays the role of Ravi describing the traditional craft; the other plays Ananya explaining her modern designs and what she hopes the blended collection will achieve. The teacher circulates and prompts with vocabulary from the chapter: artisan, furnace, geometric, intergenerational.

Word-work synthesis: the teacher writes two sentences on the board — one using past perfect, one using a chapter word without correct punctuation — and the class corrects them together, naming the grammatical feature (past perfect: 'Ravi had crafted bangles for years before Ananya joined him') and the punctuation rule (comma after introductory phrase, capital for proper noun).

Writing synthesis: children write three to four sentences in their notebooks in response to this prompt — 'If Firozabad glass bangles could be found in a new country, what would you tell people about them and the people who make them?' The teacher models the opening clause on the board; children write independently without assistance.

Beyond-text synthesis: the teacher asks children to name one Indian craft they now know more about because of this chapter's beyond-text work — Madhubani, Paithani, Blue pottery, Phulkari, or rangoli — and to say one sentence about why that craft matters to its region's people. This connects the research and hands-on craft activities to the chapter's broader argument about community and pride.

The teacher closes the chapter by returning to its central theme: skilled traditional craft, enriched by a younger generation's vision, creates beauty and livelihoods together. Two volunteers read their synthesis sentences aloud, and the teacher thanks the class for the quality of thinking the chapter provoked.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together the chapter's reading, grammar, speaking, writing, and craft-exploration threads as a unified whole, treating Ravi and Ananya's story as the conceptual spine. Children can access every band from the chapter's content alone — no prior activity needs to have happened in any particular form. Watch for children who write the synthesis prompt very literally (listing facts) rather than speaking to an imagined audience; gently redirect by asking 'What would you want that person to feel about the craft?'

items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes what Ananya brought to Ravi's workshop in Firozabad?

options.label: A
options.text: She brought a large supply of raw glass from another city.

options.label: B
options.text: She introduced modern floral and geometric patterns to complement the traditional designs.

options.label: C
options.text: She managed the packing and transportation of the bangles.

options.label: D
options.text: She replaced all the traditional designs with completely new ones.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the child focused on material supply rather than Ananya's creative contribution.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a misreading that misses the collaborative, blending nature of Ananya's work alongside tradition.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses a community-impact detail (jobs in packing and transport) with Ananya's personal role.

items.item_stem: The success of Ravi and Ananya's special Diwali bangle collection helped people beyond their workshop. Describe two ways in which the wider community benefited from this success.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The success created more work for local artisans and also generated jobs for people involved in packing and transportation of the bangles.

items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the passage below about making besan laddus. Listen carefully, then decide whether each statement is true or false and give a one-sentence reason drawn from the passage.
1. The mother was the first person to work with the chickpea flour.
2. Meera and Arjun added the ghee and sugar to the mixture.
3. The laddus were decorated with chopped nuts at the end.

options.text: Meera and Arjun added the ghee and sugar to the mixture.
The laddus were decorated with chopped nuts at the end.
The mother was the first person to work with the chickpea flour.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — the mother roasts the chickpea flour first. 2. False — the father adds ghee and sugar; Meera and Arjun shape the balls. 3. True — the kids decorate each laddu with chopped nuts as the final step.

items.item_stem: The chapter tells us that glass bangles from Firozabad are closely linked to Indian festivals, especially Diwali. Think of a craft or tradition from your own region that is connected to a festival. Speak for about one minute: name the craft or tradition, name the festival it is linked to, and explain one way it is made or performed.

expected_elements: Names a specific craft or tradition clearly.
Links it to a named festival.
Gives one accurate making or performing detail.

items.item_stem: Read the four hints below and choose two or three of them to complete this sentence: 'When I celebrate a festival, I…' — (a) a special food we make, (b) meeting family or friends, (c) a prayer or ritual we follow, (d) something we do that makes the day feel special. Choose the option that lists the hints a good festival paragraph should include.

options.label: A
options.text: A long list of every festival in India, named one after another.

options.label: B
options.text: At least two or three of the hints — food, people, prayer or ritual — woven into connected sentences.

options.label: C
options.text: Only general facts about festivals found in books, not personal experiences.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the special food we eat, because that is the most important part of any festival.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a child who has not understood the multi-angle hint scaffold and defaults to one familiar idea.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the child has conflated a list-making task with a paragraph-writing task.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the child may not have engaged with the personal-experience framing of the writing prompt.
